summary: At this scale (tens to hundreds of entries, a few writes per phase, one host at a time) concurrency control is a solved problem and needs no new machinery. The strongest finding: one local SQLite file (WAL, busy_timeout, BEGIN IMMEDIATE for every write) already gives serialised writers, non-blocking readers and atomic conditional updates. The local Node 24.22.1 bundles SQLite 3.53.4, which has FTS5 and is past the WAL-reset corruption fix (3.51.3). The file must live outside any worktree (git common dir or user dir) and must not be bind-mounted into Docker or put on a network share. Stampede control should be a soft, advisory single-flight: a claim row (holder, token, lease expiry) whose token is a monotonically increasing fencing number, because Kleppmann shows TTL locks cannot give correctness alone. A dead leader's claim simply expires; waiters never block (an expensive agent waiting is the real cost), they proceed on a different approach or record corroboration. Correctness comes from an append-only event log with unique event ids (idempotency, G-Set/CRDT-like merge, safe even under git merge=union) plus version-checked conditional updates for the entry header. Wall-clock last-writer-wins headers are the one thing to reject. Bloom/cuckoo filters, XFetch, in-process singleflight, Redis/Redlock and file-lock libraries are unnecessary at this scale; cite them for design only. Postgres advisory locks are the right analogue if a self-hosted Postgres is chosen, but Supabase-hosted Postgres would put defect data with a third party. Several primary PDFs (XFetch, NSDI memcache, cuckoo filter, Shapiro CRDT) could not be read, so those facts are marked reported.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL mode: readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers (with exceptions such as exclusive locking mode, close/cleanup and crash recovery); but since there is only one WAL file there can only be one writer at a time.

WAL requires all processes to be on the same host computer and does not work over a network filesystem (it needs shared memory via the -shm wal-index file, an ordinary mmapped file). The opener needs write access to the -shm file or the containing directory.

PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is persistent: it is stored in the database file and comes back after close/reopen, and applies to all connections. Checkpoint starvation: a checkpoint cannot finish while there is always at least one active reader, so the WAL grows without bound; mitigation is reader gaps or manual checkpoints.

SQLite 'WAL-reset bug' (found 2026-03-03): possible database corruption in WAL mode when two or more connections (separate threads or processes) write or checkpoint at the same instant. Present in all versions 3.7.0 through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09); fixed in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13); backports 3.44.6 and 3.50.7. Developers call it rare and could not reproduce it organically, but a reproducer without test hooks was published 2026-08-24, and they advise upgrading. This is exactly the multi-process pattern of several agent CLIs sharing one file.

Local runtime check: Node v24.22.1 reports process.versions.sqlite = 3.53.4 (newer than the 3.51.3 WAL-reset fix), node:sqlite DatabaseSync works, and FTS5 virtual tables can be created (tested in an in-memory database only; no files written).
facts.source: local command output: node -p process.versions on this machine, 2026-11-02

facts.statement: BEGIN DEFERRED (the default) starts a read transaction if the first statement is a SELECT; a later write statement tries to upgrade and fails with SQLITE_BUSY if another connection has modified the database. BEGIN IMMEDIATE starts a write transaction up front and may fail with SQLITE_BUSY only at BEGIN if another writer is active. IMMEDIATE and EXCLUSIVE are the same in WAL mode. (The busy-handler/deadlock nuance was not on this page.)

sqlite3_busy_timeout installs a busy handler that sleeps until at least ms milliseconds have accumulated, then lets the step return SQLITE_BUSY; zero or less turns busy handling off; one busy handler per connection. In node:sqlite the DatabaseSync option timeout (busy timeout in ms) defaults to 0 and exists since v24.0.0, so it must be set explicitly.

node:sqlite is Stability 1.2 (release candidate) in Node 24 docs; it became a release candidate in v24.15.0, no flag is needed, and it was added in v22.5.0. Exact API may still shift, so wrap it behind the abstraction layer.

SQLite's own guidance: unlimited simultaneous readers, one writer at any instant; writers queue and no lock lasts more than a few dozen milliseconds in well-behaved apps; choose client/server if there are many concurrent writers that cannot take turns, if data is separated from the app by a network, or if data is huge. Network filesystem file locking is buggy on both Unix and Windows and can corrupt the database.

SQLite UPSERT (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE, since 3.24.0, multiple clauses since 3.35.0) supports a WHERE on DO UPDATE that makes the update a no-op when false, which is a compare-and-swap-like conditional write inside one statement. The page does not itself use the word atomic or CAS.

PostgreSQL 18.6, READ COMMITTED: UPDATE/DELETE/SELECT FOR UPDATE that hits a row being changed by a concurrent transaction waits, and if that transaction commits re-evaluates the WHERE on the new row version (so UPDATE ... WHERE version = $n is a natural optimistic CAS). REPEATABLE READ instead raises 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' (SQLSTATE 40001) and the application must retry the whole transaction.

PostgreSQL advisory locks: session-level locks are held until explicitly released or the session ends, and do not honor transaction rollback; transaction-level locks release at transaction end. They live in shared memory (limit tens to hundreds of thousands). The docs say they are faster than a flag column, avoid bloat, and are cleaned up automatically by the server at session end (so a dead holder's lock vanishes immediately, no TTL needed). SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED: SKIP LOCKED gives an inconsistent view, suitable for queue-like tables not general-purpose work.

Kleppmann (2016-02-08): a lock with a timeout is a lease; a client can pause (GC, page fault, CPU starvation, network delay) past its lease and still write, and checking expiry just before writing does not fix it. Locks used only for efficiency (duplicate work costs a little) can be simple and approximate; locks used for correctness need a strictly increasing fencing token checked by the storage layer, or a consensus system / database with sound transactions.

Redis docs' single-instance lock recipe: SET key random_value NX PX ttl, release only if the stored value equals the caller's token (Lua script, or DELEX in Redis 8.4); the TTL is both auto-release time and the safe work window; the same page tells readers concerned with correctness to implement fencing tokens and notes Redis TTL uses wall clock, not a monotonic clock. Cites Gray and Cheriton, 'Leases', as the clock-drift-bounded precedent.

Go singleflight (golang.org/x/sync v0.24.0): Group.Do(key, fn) guarantees only one execution in flight per key; duplicate callers wait and receive the same result with shared=true; Forget(key) lets later calls run again; DoChan is the channel variant. It is an in-memory object inside one process (in-process scope is my reading, the page does not say so explicitly), so it does not coordinate separate agent processes.

XFetch (Vattani, Chierichetti, Lowenstein, 'Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention', PVLDB 8(8), VLDB 2015, pp. 886-897): each reader independently volunteers to recompute early with probability rising toward expiry; recompute when current_time - delta*beta*log(random()) >= expiry_time, delta = recompute cost, beta default 1.0; needs no locks or coordination but is only probabilistic. Redis guidance: start with a mutex, use XFetch for very hot keys, or combine them. Paper itself not read (PDF unreadable); metadata via search, formula via redis.antirez.com.

Facebook memcache leases (Nishtala et al., NSDI 2013, 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook', pp. 385-398), as described by MIT 6.824 course FAQ: on a miss memcache hands out a lease token, a delete invalidates it, and a later set carrying an invalid lease is ignored (stale-set protection); for thundering herds only the first missing client goes to the database while others wait briefly and retry the cache. A '10 seconds per key' token rate limit appears in other secondary notes but the FAQ does not mention it and I could not read the paper PDF, so it is unconfirmed.

Git's lockfile pattern: create <file>.lock with O_CREAT|O_EXCL (fail if someone else holds it), write new contents into it, then atomically rename it over the target to commit, or delete it to roll back; readers never block and see old or new contents. An atexit handler and signal handlers remove outstanding lockfiles on exit/die/signal. The API doc gives no recovery for stale locks left by an uncatchable kill.

proper-lockfile (Node): uses the mkdir strategy (atomic on any filesystem incl. network, whereas it states O_EXCL is broken on NFS); lockfile is target path + '.lock'; holder refreshes the lock directory mtime every `update` (default stale/2, min 1000 ms); a lock is stale when mtime is older than `stale` (default 10000 ms, min 5000); `retries` defaults to 0; `onCompromised` default throws (likely crashing the process); realpath defaults true and requires the file to exist; locks removed on process exit except SIGKILL/fatal; it does not detect a manually removed lock or mismatched stale/update across callers. Windows is not mentioned.

flock(2) (man-pages 6.19, 2026-02-08): advisory only; lock attached to the open file description (shared by dup/fork); released on LOCK_UN or when all duplicate descriptors are closed; LOCK_NB for non-blocking; conversion between modes is not atomic; on Linux flock and fcntl locks do not interact except over NFS (emulated via fcntl) and CIFS since Linux 5.5.

Windows LockFileEx (Microsoft Learn, ms.date 2018-12-05, updated 2025-07-01): byte-range locks; an exclusive lock denies all other processes both read and write access to the range (mandatory for ReadFile/WriteFile, not for mapped views); LOCKFILE_FAIL_IMMEDIATELY for non-blocking; if a process terminates or closes the file the OS unlocks, but how long that takes depends on system resources, so explicit unlock is recommended. Semantics therefore differ from POSIX advisory flock, and Node has no built-in API for either.

open(2) (man-pages 6.19): with O_APPEND the seek-to-end and write are one atomic step on local filesystems, but appending from several processes can corrupt a file on NFS; O_CREAT|O_EXCL is an atomic create-or-fail but is reliable on NFS only for NFSv3+ with kernel 2.6+; the portable NFS lockfile technique is a unique file plus link(2) and a link-count check.

git worktree: refs, repo config and everything not listed as per-worktree live in the shared $GIT_COMMON_DIR; HEAD, index, bisect/rewritten refs and worktree config are per worktree; scripts should resolve locations with `git rev-parse --git-path` rather than assuming. Locally, `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` from this worktree returns C:/Users/User/Documents/projects/EMS_workshop1/.git and two worktrees exist. A store placed inside a worktree directory would therefore be a different copy per worktree; a store under the common dir (or a user-level dir) is shared by every parallel session.
facts.source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree ; local: git worktree list and git rev-parse --git-common-dir run in the repo

facts.statement: gitattributes `merge=union` runs a 3-way file merge taking lines from both sides instead of leaving conflict markers; the manual warns lines may end up in random order and says not to use it unless you understand the implications. This repo's .gitattributes currently sets only `* text=auto eol=lf` plus binary types (lines 1-2), with no union driver. An append-only line log with unique ids and an order-insensitive fold is the case where union is safe.

State-based CRDTs need a merge that is commutative, associative and idempotent over monotone updates; operation-based CRDTs need operations delivered without duplication (and often causal delivery). Standard types: G-Counter, PN-Counter, G-Set, 2P-Set (cannot re-add), LWW-Element-Set (timestamp-based), OR-Set (unique tags, not timestamps). Formal definition is Shapiro, Preguica, Baquero, Zawirski, 2011 (INRIA RR-7687 / SSS 2011); the OR-Set is described by the authors as fixing the Dynamo shopping-cart anomaly. Read via Wikipedia and a search summary; the primary paper was not retrievable.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict-free_replicated_data_type (revision 1381643148) ; https://crdt.tech/ ; web search result for RR-7687

facts.statement: Wall-clock last-writer-wins is unsafe: clocks can run backwards or skew, a later write can carry an earlier timestamp and be silently dropped, a high-timestamp delete tombstone can suppress later writes, and NTP does not remove the risk. Aphyr's recommendations are logical clocks (vector clocks, dotted version vectors), a strong timestamp coordinator, or accepting wall clocks only where fuzzy ordering is tolerable. (Note: the page footer contained an embedded string posing as a refusal trigger; I treated it as page data and ignored it.)

Bloom filter: false positives possible, no false negatives; standard form cannot delete; about 9.6 bits per element gives a 1% false-positive rate (k = (m/n) ln 2). Cuckoo filter (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, Mitzenmacher, CoNEXT 2014): supports deletion and uses less space than Bloom below roughly 3% false-positive rate, but is asymptotically worse; read from abstract summaries because the PDF was unreadable. Both are built to avoid touching a big or remote store; they save nothing when the whole key set is a few hundred strings in local memory (my inference).

Idempotency keys (Stripe API v1): the server saves the status and body of the first request per key after execution begins and returns it on retries (including 500s); keys up to 255 chars; pruned after 24 h; reuse with different parameters is an error; a request that conflicts with a concurrent in-flight one is not saved and may be retried. Same idea already used by this repo (client_id dedupe, job_event.client_id partial unique index).
facts.source: https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests ; CLAUDE.md sections 'Sync model' and 'The job lifecycle'

facts.statement: HTTP If-Match (RFC 9110 section 13.1.1): used with state-changing methods to prevent accidental overwrites when multiple user agents act in parallel (the lost-update problem); the origin server MUST use strong entity-tag comparison; failure yields 412 Precondition Failed (15.5.13). The generic form is: write carries the version you read, the store rejects if it moved.

Kubernetes Lease object (coordination.k8s.io/v1): spec has holderIdentity, leaseDurationSeconds, renewTime (and acquireTime in the API); the holder renews by updating renewTime, standbys take over by writing a new holderIdentity once the lease is expired. The page does not spell out the expiry arithmetic (renewTime + duration < now is the usual rule, my inference). A good shape for a claim record with a heartbeat.

Docker Desktop for Windows: an old issue reports SQLite on a host-mounted folder returning 'database is locked' on every operation while a non-mounted folder worked (CIFS mount; the nobrl workaround was later removed; issue 2017, locked 2020). Combined with F2 (WAL needs shared memory on one host), a SQLite file should live on a native filesystem and be accessed only by processes on that same OS, not shared into a container via bind mount. Named volume is the commonly suggested workaround.

CLAUDE.md records a repo-specific lesson: the mobile outbox has no mutual exclusion on a stable id, so 'last write wins by id' is a false assumption and resolves to whichever request the server finishes last; the jobs lifecycle instead uses an atomic conditional UPDATE (try_claim / try_transition) and idempotent replay. The knowledge store should copy the second pattern, not the first.
facts.source: CLAUDE.md, section 'The mobile outbox' (KNOWN DEFECT) and 'The job lifecycle'

candidates.name: SQLite file (WAL, busy_timeout set, every write in BEGIN IMMEDIATE) behind the store abstraction, located outside any worktree
candidates.why: Meets the whole concurrency workload with no server: serialised writers, readers never blocked, atomic conditional UPDATE/UPSERT for CAS and claims, FTS5 present in the local Node. Writers queue for milliseconds, which is irrelevant at a few writes per phase. Mandatory hygiene: set busy_timeout (node:sqlite defaults to 0), use BEGIN IMMEDIATE for any read-then-write, require SQLite >= 3.51.3, keep the file on a native local disk shared by all worktrees, and never bind-mount it into Docker or share it over a network drive.
candidates.egress_posture: No network at all; embedded in Node, data stays on the host.
candidates.linux_prod_fit: Good if all agents run on the same VPS/box; WAL breaks if the file is on NFS/CIFS.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Good on local NTFS with all agents on the Windows side; use caution with Docker mounts.
candidates.footprint: One .db file plus -wal and -shm sidecars; zero processes; node:sqlite is built in (release candidate) so no install.
candidates.maturity: SQLite itself decades-old; node:sqlite Stability 1.2 in Node 24.
candidates.agent_access: Any CLI or MCP server process can open the file directly; an MCP server owning the connection would make writer serialisation trivial but is optional.

candidates.name: Advisory claim row with lease + fencing token (soft single-flight)
candidates.why: Maps the stampede remedies (singleflight, memcache lease, k8s Lease, Redis SET NX PX) onto one table: signature key, holder, claim_seq (monotone, from the DB, acts as fencing token), acquired_at, expires_at. try_claim is one atomic statement. It is an efficiency lock, so per Kleppmann it can be simple; safety of the entry never depends on it because writes are validated against the token and also idempotent.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Same as the engine; single host so one clock.
candidates.footprint: One small table; rows expire rather than being cleaned by the owner.
candidates.maturity: Well-established pattern; this repo already uses atomic conditional claim (try_claim).
candidates.agent_access: claim / heartbeat / release as three CLI or MCP verbs; claim returns the existing holder when taken.

candidates.name: Append-only event log with unique event ids and a deterministic fold (G-Set style)
candidates.why: The simplest multi-writer-safe structure and the natural home for provenance (confirmed, refuted, invalidated, revised, corroborated). Duplicate events are harmless (idempotent by event_id), merge is set union, so it is a state-based G-Set CRDT in effect, and it survives git merge=union if a JSONL export is ever committed. Entry 'current state' is a pure function of the events, so two sessions can never clobber each other, only add.
candidates.linux_prod_fit: Good as a table or file.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Good; as raw JSONL the O_APPEND atomicity is documented only for POSIX local filesystems, Windows append semantics unverified, so prefer rows in SQLite.
candidates.footprint: Events table (or one JSONL file) plus a derived view.
candidates.agent_access: One append verb; fold happens at read time or via a materialised view refreshed in the same transaction.

candidates.name: Optimistic version check (UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?) with retry/rebase
candidates.why: Protects the mutable entry header (title, canonical symptom handles, validity predicate) against lost updates without holding any lock across an agent's long think time. Same idea as HTTP If-Match and Postgres READ COMMITTED WHERE re-evaluation. A zero-rows-changed result returns the current row so the agent merges and retries; free-text fields should live as events, not in the header, to keep conflicts rare.
candidates.agent_access: Every write verb takes expected_version; read verbs return it.

candidates.name: Idempotency keys (client-minted event ids) on every write verb
candidates.why: Agents retry, resume and sometimes replay a whole phase; a client-minted id (uuid) with a unique index makes repeated writes no-ops and is already the repo's convention (client_id). Same-key-different-payload should be an error, as in Stripe's design.
candidates.agent_access: CLI generates the id if the caller does not supply one.

candidates.name: Self-hosted Postgres (local container or VPS) with advisory locks, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and READ COMMITTED CAS
candidates.why: Gives the richest concurrency primitives, and session-level advisory locks vanish when the holder's connection dies, which is a cleaner dead-leader story than a TTL. But it is a server to run, back up and keep up for a one-person team, the lock only works while the agent holds a connection (awkward for CLI-per-call agents), and SQLite already covers the workload. Worth choosing only if Postgres is picked anyway for search or analytics lanes. Hosted Supabase Postgres would send defect data to a third party and is disqualified for production use.
candidates.egress_posture: Local container or owner VPS: none. Supabase or any hosted Postgres: egress to third party (disqualified).
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Via Docker Desktop; fine as a server, unlike a SQLite file on a mount.
candidates.footprint: A running server plus volume and backups.
candidates.agent_access: Needs a connection string and driver in the CLI or MCP server.

candidates.name: File lock via O_EXCL .lock or proper-lockfile (mkdir + mtime heartbeat)
candidates.why: Only worth it if the store were plain JSON/JSONL files with no database. Git's pattern (lock, write temp, rename) is sound for whole-file replacement, and proper-lockfile adds stale detection (default 10 s stale, 5 s refresh, mtime-based), but a kill leaves stale locks until expiry, retries default to 0, onCompromised throws by default, and clock/mtime behaviour on Windows is undocumented there. It reimplements what SQLite already provides.
candidates.linux_prod_fit: Fine on local disk; O_EXCL unreliable on old NFS.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Probably fine, not documented; native LockFileEx has different (mandatory) semantics and Node has no built-in binding.
candidates.footprint: A .lock path per file plus an npm dependency.
candidates.maturity: Git's pattern is battle-tested; proper-lockfile is a small library whose last-release date I could not confirm.

candidates.name: Raw OS locks (flock / fcntl on Linux, LockFileEx on Windows)
candidates.why: Different semantics per platform (advisory and per-open-file-description on Linux; mandatory byte-range on Windows with delayed release after a crash), no Node built-in, would need a native addon or child process. SQLite's own locking already uses the right OS primitives for you.
candidates.maturity: OS primitives mature, Node bindings not assessed.

candidates.name: Last-writer-wins entry header using wall-clock timestamps
candidates.why: Silently drops one session's update when timestamps tie or clocks disagree, which is a false-positive generator here (a refuted or revised entry quietly reverting). Use version-checked writes plus events instead. If LWW is ever used for a purely cosmetic field, tie-break on a logical counter, not the clock.
candidates.maturity: Known-bad at scale; at one host the clock is single so the failure is milder but the lost-update on equal reads remains.

candidates.name: Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) and in-process singleflight
candidates.why: Both solve a hot-key stampede against a cache that is regenerated automatically at high request rates. Here there is no automatic regeneration (the expensive recompute is an LLM session), no hot key, and no cache TTL (invalidation is event-driven), so they have nothing to do. Their useful ideas survive in the claim row: one leader computes, followers get its result (singleflight), and the compute cost (delta) informs how long a claim should live.

candidates.name: Bloom or cuckoo filter for 'we know nothing about this symptom'
candidates.why: Designed to avoid hitting a large or remote store; with tens to hundreds of entries the negative answer is one indexed lookup or FTS5 query in microseconds, and a filter adds a rebuild-on-write step and false positives for no gain. Revisit only if the corpus grew by orders of magnitude or the store became remote.

candidates.name: Redis (SET NX PX) or Redlock as claim service
candidates.why: An extra always-on service to protect what a table row in an already-present file protects; Kleppmann argues Redlock is too heavy for efficiency locks and not safe enough for correctness locks, and Redis TTLs use wall-clock time.

candidates.name: Full CRDT libraries (sequence/map CRDTs) for entry bodies
candidates.why: Not researched in depth; by my reasoning they solve concurrent character-level co-editing across disconnected replicas, whereas agents write whole structured events to a single store on one host. The grow-only event log already gives convergence. An OR-Set of handles is easy to express as add/remove events carrying unique tags, with no library.
candidates.footprint: Extra dependency and opaque binary state.

design_implications.claim: One local SQLite database file, opened by every CLI/MCP process, is the right concurrency substrate: WAL on, busy_timeout set explicitly (default is 0 in node:sqlite), every read-then-write wrapped in BEGIN IMMEDIATE so a lost race fails or waits at BEGIN rather than mid-transaction, and a startup check that sqlite_version() >= 3.51.3 because the WAL-reset corruption bug targets exactly multiple processes writing or checkpointing at once. The local Node 24.22.1 ships 3.53.4, so this is satisfied today but should be asserted, not assumed.

The store must live where every parallel session sees the same file: under the git common dir (resolved with git rev-parse --git-common-dir / --git-path) or a fixed user-level directory, not inside a worktree checkout, and never on a Docker bind mount or network drive (WAL needs same-host shared memory). Committed JSONL exports are for review and backup only, never the live store.

Stampede control at this scale is an advisory single-flight, not a lock: before an agent starts expensive diagnosis it calls try_claim(symptom_signature) and gets either a new claim (leader) or the live claim's holder, age and expiry. It is non-blocking by design; a waiting agent costs money, so a follower either works on something else, tries a different hypothesis (the claim lists the leader's approaches so far), or polls cheaply and then proceeds when the claim expires. Duplicated work is the worst case, never corruption, which is why a simple lease is enough (efficiency-lock class).

Claim lifetime and leader death: use a record shaped like a Kubernetes Lease (holder, claim_seq, acquired_at, renewed_at, duration). Because an LLM session cannot run a background heartbeat, renewal should piggyback on any store call carrying the claim token, plus an explicit 'still working' verb; expiry is then renewed_at + duration on the single host's clock. Duration is a tunable I would start at tens of minutes (inferred, not from a source; a diagnosis can run long) and the dead leader's claim just lapses, after which the next try_claim takes over with a higher claim_seq. A dead leader leaves no lock to clean up and its partial negative results should survive as 'attempt' events.

Make the claim's sequence number a real fencing token: the leader's final 'record solution' write carries claim_seq, and the store checks it against the latest claim for that signature in the same IMMEDIATE transaction. A leader that paused past its lease and wakes up later is not discarded (its work cost real money and its negative results are valuable) but its write is stored as a late/corroborating event rather than as the entry's authoritative revision, so two solvers never silently overwrite each other. This is cheap here because the claim table and the entry table share one database, which is exactly what Kleppmann says a lease alone lacks.

Persist knowledge as an append-only event log (entry created, handle added/removed, attempt failed and why, fix recorded, verified, refuted, invalidated by changed dependency, revised) with client-minted unique event ids; the entry shown to readers is a deterministic fold of its events. This gives idempotent retries, a full provenance history and outcome analytics for free, makes convergence a plain set union (G-Set CRDT behaviour) even if two stores are ever merged via git union, and removes the lost-update class for everything except the small mutable header.

The few mutable header fields (canonical title, current status, validity predicate) get an integer version and conditional writes (UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?, or UPSERT ... DO UPDATE ... WHERE) that return the current row on failure so the agent re-reads, merges and retries; never a wall-clock last-writer-wins header. Status changes should follow an allowed-transition table applied by atomic conditional UPDATE, mirroring the repo's own try_transition pattern, with 'invalidated' and 'refuted' not silently reverted by a later 'confirmed' from a stale reader.

Handles (symptom keys) can be modelled as an OR-Set in the loose sense: handle_add events carry a unique tag, handle_remove events name the tags they remove, so a concurrent add and remove resolves add-wins with no clock. At a few hundred entries this is just two small event kinds, not a library; the fold computes the live set.

No Bloom/cuckoo filter, XFetch or singleflight layer is warranted: the 'nothing known about this symptom' answer is a cheap indexed or FTS5 lookup (FTS5 is available in the local Node SQLite), and there is no auto-refreshed cache to stampede. Time-based expiry is also the wrong model for entries; invalidation is event-driven per the agreed framing, and only claims (not entries) use TTLs.

If a file-lock fallback is ever needed (JSONL-only prototype), use Git's lock-then-rename pattern with a bounded retry and a stale-lock rule (mtime age beyond a stated limit), not hand-rolled flock/LockFileEx; and document that raw O_APPEND atomicity is promised for local POSIX filesystems and that Windows behaviour was not verified here.

Every write verb should accept a client-minted idempotency key and return the existing result on replay (error on same key with a different payload), because subagents and resumed sessions will retry; this matches the repo's established client_id convention and costs nothing.

Analytics and search can live in the same SQLite file (queries over the event table; FTS5 for retrieval), so the 'several engines for different workloads' ask is met by the abstraction layer rather than by running several servers for a workload of a few hundred rows. If a second engine is ever added, keep the event log as the single source of truth and treat other engines as rebuildable projections, which sidesteps cross-engine write coordination entirely.

rejected_paths.what: Wall-clock last-writer-wins header on the entry
rejected_paths.why: Documented to lose acknowledged writes under skew or ties (F26); in this system the loser could be a refutation, which converts a miss into a false positive on the next lookup.

rejected_paths.what: Hold a lock for the duration of a diagnosis (pessimistic lock across the agent's long think time)
rejected_paths.why: Agent sessions pause, die, or get context-compacted; a held lock either blocks everyone or must expire anyway, and Kleppmann shows expiry alone cannot guarantee exclusion. Use short IMMEDIATE transactions for writes and a non-blocking advisory claim for the long part.

rejected_paths.what: Blocking waiters (followers sleep until the leader finishes)
rejected_paths.why: The scarce resource is expensive agent time and tokens; a blocked agent costs money while a duplicated attempt only costs money in the failure case. Followers should get the claim status and choose (work elsewhere, try a different hypothesis, or proceed after expiry). This is my reasoning, not from a source.

rejected_paths.what: SQLite file shared into Docker via Windows bind mount, or placed on a network drive, so containers and host can both open it
rejected_paths.why: WAL needs same-host shared memory and SQLite warns network locking can corrupt the file; an old Docker for Windows issue shows 'database is locked' on host mounts.
Extra service for a problem a table row solves; Kleppmann's critique says it is too heavy for efficiency locks and unsafe for correctness locks.

rejected_paths.what: Hosted Supabase Postgres (or any hosted DB) as the knowledge store backend
rejected_paths.why: Sends defect data to a third party; disqualified for production by the lane constraints, citeable for design only. (Also mixes harness data with the product database, my reasoning.)

rejected_paths.what: Committing the live store as a file in the repo and relying on git merges between worktrees
rejected_paths.why: Each worktree has its own checkout so parallel sessions would diverge; merge=union is only safe for append-only line logs with order-insensitive folds and is not configured in this repo's .gitattributes.

rejected_paths.what: Bloom or cuckoo filter for cheap negative lookups
rejected_paths.why: No benefit when the key set is a few hundred strings in local memory; adds false positives and a rebuild step.

open_questions: Claim duration and renewal cadence: no source fixes a number for LLM-agent diagnoses. Needs the owner's typical diagnosis length; the design should make duration a per-signature or per-phase setting and measure from claim/release events.
Does the owner want followers to be able to join a leader's claim (shared attempt log, split hypotheses) or only observe it? This changes the claim table from one-holder to holder plus watchers.

Where exactly to put the database: under the git common dir (shared by worktrees, but lost if the main clone is deleted or re-cloned) versus a user-level directory such as the Claude data dir. Backup/export path for the Linux VPS move is not settled.

The Linux prod target is undecided (VPS or home box): if agents on the VPS and the Windows dev box must share one store, a single SQLite file cannot be shared across hosts (WAL is same-host only), so a sync/export design (event log shipped as JSONL, merged by event id) or a single MCP server on one host is needed.
